title: Symmetry-breaking chelation enables room-temperature all-optical spin coherence readout of aqueous Cu(II) for chemoselective discrimination
authors: Jinlei Li, Qiaoyun Wu, Qiaoqiao Shao, Zhubin Hu, Haitao Sun, Zhenrong Sun, Donghai Feng
abstract: Optical initialization and readout of molecular electron spins in water remains challenging for 3d transition-metal complexes. Their Laporte-forbidden d-d transitions yield weak transition dipole moments, so optical spin detection in aqueous Cu(II) previously required ~1 M concentrations. Here we overcome this constraint through symmetry-breaking chelation. Coordinating Cu(II) with EDTA imposes a non-centrosymmetric ligand field with enhanced metal-ligand covalency, relaxing Laporte restrictions and amplifying d-d transition dipole moments. This design enhances absorption and magnetic circular dichroism by 7.3- and 5.6-fold, enabling ultrafast spin readout down to 100 μM with an apparent dephasing time T2^*~0.54 ns. As a proof-of-concept for selective molecular-spin sensing, histidine addition extends T_2^* to ~0.8 ns in a concentration-dependent manner, whereas glycine produces no measurable effect. These results show that symmetry breaking provides a strategy to create molecular spin-photon interfaces, opening avenues toward all-optical, analyte-responsive quantum sensing in water.
summary: The authors overcome the difficulty of optically reading electron spins in aqueous Cu(II) by using EDTA chelation to break symmetry, significantly enhancing optical signals. They then demonstrate that spin coherence time can be measured at low concentrations and, critically, that this coherence time can be selectively extended by binding to specific amino acids like histidine, opening avenues for quantum sensing.
main_problem: Optical spin readout of aqueous Cu(II) is challenging due to weak, Laporte-forbidden d-d transitions, historically requiring high concentrations.
main_result: Symmetry-breaking chelation with EDTA enhances optical signals and enables ultrafast, low-concentration spin readout, while specific ligands like histidine can chemoselectively extend spin coherence time.
method: The study combines advanced spectroscopic measurements (MCD, pump-probe) with quantum chemical calculations (DFT, TD-DFT) to model electronic structure and spin dynamics.
model_or_system: The system is aqueous Cu(II) complexes, specifically comparing the aqua ion to those chelated by EDTA, and further testing selectivity using histidine and glycine ligands.
key_observables: Spin dephasing time (T2*), magnetic circular dichroism (MCD) amplitude, and UV-vis absorption enhancement factors.
important_parameters: Low concentrations ($\sim 100 \mu	ext{M}$), room temperature, and varying transverse magnetic fields ($B_\perp$).
main_assumptions: The initial aqua ion model is treated as time-averaged, and the spin dynamics are analyzed using pump-probe spectroscopy techniques.
figures_summary: Figures show spectral enhancements (MCD/UV-vis) comparing complexes, time-resolved spin coherence decay curves across concentrations, and plots detailing the linear dependence of $1/T_2^*$ on $B_\perp$ and the concentration-dependent extension of $T_2^*$ upon histidine addition.
paper_structure: The paper first establishes the spectroscopic enhancement mechanism via symmetry breaking (EDTA vs. aqua). It then uses time-resolved pump-probe spectroscopy to demonstrate low-concentration spin readout. Finally, it performs detailed analysis showing that ligand binding (His vs. Gly) modulates the spin coherence time in a chemically specific manner.
why_interesting: This work provides a direct, experimentally validated platform for using molecular spin coherence as a highly sensitive, all-optical sensor for chemical species in aqueous media, bridging quantum optics with biochemistry.
